preconditions: Vault is configured with a plugin directory (plugin_directory) and a file audit device whose file_path/path points inside that directory.

The malicious audit device config is PERSISTED (written to Vault's storage barrier) so it is reconstructed on startup/unseal via newAuditBackendWithFormatter() rather than going through enableAudit() — i.e. the attacker has storage-write access, or a backup/restore or replication path injects the entry.
On restart, the persisted device is reconstructed WITHOUT the plugin-directory guard and the file sink opens a log file inside the plugin directory.

evidence.vulnerable_version: vault <= v2.2.2 (latest release, tag c56e7e6, 2026-11-12); the guard lives only in enableAudit()
evidence.fixed_version: unreleased (main only; 60c9bcca2 merged 2026-11-19, not in v2.2.2)
evidence.observed_result: poc.go transcribes the fixed validateAuditFileDestination() verbatim and contrasts it with v2.2.2's newAuditBackendWithFormatter() (no guard). With a file audit path inside the plugin directory, the vulnerable path accepts it and the file sink writes the audit log INTO the plugin directory (escaped=true); the fixed validation returns 'audit file target may not be in the plugin directory'.

real_exploit.target: hashicorp/vault — vault/audit.go: the plugin-directory guard (enableAudit L136-158) is not applied at backend construction (newAuditBackendWithFormatter L552), so persisted file audit devices bypass it and write into the plugin directory
real_exploit.backend: a self-contained Go driver reproducing the exact fixed validateAuditFileDestination() logic (verbatim from 60c9bcca2) and the vulnerable v2.2.2 construction path against a real temp plugin directory
real_exploit.demonstrated: The vulnerable path writes an audit log file into the plugin directory (the isolation boundary the guard protects, and the RCE/plugin-injection surface); the fixed validation rejects the same path.
